frictionVectors.title: European Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong control through Sonatrach, but European buyers seek alternative gas supplies and greater investment access. Hydrocarbon dependence remains a structural vulnerability to external price and demand shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Morocco-Sahel Strategic Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Tensions with Morocco and instability across the Sahel complicate border security, trade corridors, and regional energy diplomacy. External powers are competing for influence around Algeria's southern periphery.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Oil Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Angola retains formal ownership of petroleum resources, but production, financing, and technical capacity remain heavily tied to international energy companies. Declining output and debt exposure constrain sovereign bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Corridor Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor is attracting United States, European, and Chinese interest because of its access to copper and cobalt supply chains. Infrastructure competition could improve connectivity while reinforcing external control over export routes.

frictionVectors.title: Niger Trade Disruption
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Niger have strained cross-border commerce and complicated the use of Benin's port and pipeline infrastructure. Regional sanctions and political disputes continue to expose Benin to decisions made beyond its borders.

frictionVectors.title: Northern Security Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity from the Sahel is pressuring northern communities, transport routes, and protected areas. Benin is expanding security cooperation, but reliance on external training and equipment creates long-term sovereignty trade-offs.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond Market Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Botswana exercises unusually strong influence through its partnership with De Beers, but remains exposed to global diamond demand and synthetic-stone competition. Negotiating greater domestic value addition remains a central sovereignty challenge.

frictionVectors.title: New-Mineral Investment Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Interest in copper, nickel, lithium, and other minerals is increasing competition among foreign investors. Botswana's regulatory capacity gives it leverage, though accelerated development could test environmental and local-benefit safeguards.

frictionVectors.title: Artisanal Gold Control
frictionVectors.details: The military government is seeking greater state control over gold production, trading, and refining, while informal extraction and illicit networks remain extensive. Russian security cooperation may increase regime autonomy but could create new opaque resource dependencies.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-Corridor Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence threatens mines, transport routes, and agricultural zones, limiting the state's ability to secure resource-producing regions. The withdrawal of Western partners has narrowed Burkina Faso's security options even as external influence from Russia and regional allies grows.

highlights: Mining reform seeks greater state control

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda-Burundi Border Tensions
frictionVectors.details: Political and security tensions with Rwanda disrupt border commerce and complicate access to regional transport and energy networks.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Nickel and rare-earth prospects attract external investors, but limited domestic processing capacity risks leaving Burundi dependent on concession-based exports.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Airfield Competition
frictionVectors.details: External partners seek influence over maritime, airport, and logistics infrastructure as Cabo Verde gains importance along Atlantic routes.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Utility Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on foreign financing for desalination, renewable energy, and transport infrastructure creates long-term exposure despite strong governance.

highlights: Oil and timber remain externally contested

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction remain important for roads, ports, and power projects, increasing repayment and strategic-access concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Resource Governance and Separatist Conflict
frictionVectors.details: Oil, timber, and mining revenues are concentrated within a fragile political system, while conflict in the Anglophone regions threatens transport corridors and local control.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security-Mining Nexus
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security actors retain influence around regime protection and mineral activity, limiting transparent state oversight of gold and diamond concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on routes through Cameroon and neighboring states leaves resource exports vulnerable to insecurity, customs bottlenecks, and foreign-controlled logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-Sector Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon revenues remain central to state finances, while foreign operators and limited domestic refining capacity constrain national control over the value chain.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The drawdown or restructuring of foreign military partnerships increases pressure on Chad to secure borders, pipelines, and trade routes with limited domestic capacity.

frictionVectors.title: France–Comoros territorial dispute
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved status of Mayotte remains a persistent sovereignty issue, intensified by migration pressures and competing claims over maritime jurisdiction.

frictionVectors.title: Connectivity and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Comoros relies heavily on external partners for ports, telecommunications, energy, and budget support, leaving limited room for independent infrastructure policy.

highlights: Critical minerals draw competing outside powers

frictionVectors.title: M23 conflict and regional intervention
frictionVectors.details: Armed conflict in the east continues to weaken state authority and expose Kinshasa to pressure from Rwanda, regional actors, and international security initiatives.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic minerals and contract leverage
frictionVectors.details: Cobalt, copper, and other critical minerals attract Chinese, Western, and Gulf-backed interests, while weak oversight limits the state's ability to convert extraction into broad public gains.

highlights: Debt and infrastructure shape external alignment

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon concentration
frictionVectors.details: The economy and state finances remain highly dependent on oil production, leaving sovereignty vulnerable to price cycles and foreign operator influence.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure and debt exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, ports, and construction projects provide essential capacity but can constrain policy flexibility through financing and repayment obligations.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa and commodity dependence
frictionVectors.details: Côte d’Ivoire is improving processing and regulatory capacity, but foreign buyers and volatile global prices still capture much of the value generated by cocoa exports.

frictionVectors.title: Competing external infrastructure partners
frictionVectors.details: French, Chinese, Gulf, and multilateral financing support major transport and energy projects, creating opportunity while increasing competition over strategic assets and standards.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military-base concentration
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti monetizes its position at the Red Sea through multiple foreign military facilities, but the arrangement limits strategic autonomy and makes the country vulnerable to regional escalation.

frictionVectors.title: Ports, debt, and Ethiopia dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed port infrastructure and Ethiopia-linked trade provide critical revenue, while debt exposure and dependence on Ethiopian cargo flows constrain national bargaining power.

highlights: Suez remains a strategic revenue shield

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Gulf Capital Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign currency shortages and refinancing needs increase leverage for Gulf investors, multilateral lenders, and strategic asset acquisitions. Cairo retains control of core infrastructure but faces narrowing policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile Allocation
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved Nile water dispute with Ethiopia remains a direct sovereignty and food-security concern. Egypt is combining diplomacy, regional partnerships, and security signaling to protect historical water access.

highlights: Oil rents are entering structural decline
Malabo seeks tighter control of offshore assets

frictionVectors.title: Mature Hydrocarbon Fields
frictionVectors.details: Declining production and dependence on foreign technical operators constrain state revenue and bargaining power. New gas and petrochemical projects offer partial relief but remain capital- and technology-dependent.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, ports, and public facilities expand connectivity while creating long-term financial and operational dependencies. Malabo is attempting to preserve sovereign control through centralized contracting and security oversight.

highlights: Red Sea geography is the core national asset

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea Port Competition
frictionVectors.details: Regional powers view Eritrean coastline and port access as strategic assets amid militarization of the Red Sea. Asmara seeks revenue and leverage without surrendering control over bases or maritime infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and Sanctions Exposure
frictionVectors.details: International mining partnerships provide essential foreign exchange but expose the state to governance, labor, and sanctions-related pressure. Limited diversification leaves resource sovereignty vulnerable to external commodity and compliance regimes.

highlights: South African corridors anchor the economy
Sugar and logistics remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: South African Economic Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Trade routes, electricity links, finance, and labor flows are heavily tied to South Africa. This dependence limits Mbabane's room to maneuver when regional supply or political pressures intensify.

frictionVectors.title: SACU Revenue Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Customs-pool receipts and preferential market access remain vital to fiscal stability. Changes in regional trade patterns or South African policy could reduce sovereign budget flexibility.

highlights: Port access remains the strategic pressure point

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea Access and Somaliland
frictionVectors.details: Ethiopia's search for reliable maritime access has intensified competition with Somalia and regional powers. Any port arrangement must balance commercial needs against sovereignty disputes and the risk of military escalation.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-built infrastructure and external debt restructuring constrain Addis Ababa's fiscal autonomy. The government is seeking diversified financing and greater domestic control while managing pressure from creditors and strategic partners.

highlights: Oil and manganese remain foreign-capital dependent

frictionVectors.title: Resource-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The post-Bongo authorities are seeking greater state participation and transparency in oil and manganese while still relying on foreign operators, creating tension over contracts and revenue capture.

frictionVectors.title: Atlantic infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Rail, ports, and mining logistics remain closely tied to external financiers and operators, limiting Libreville's ability to rapidly nationalize or redirect mineral supply chains.

highlights: Senegal remains the strategic economic anchor

frictionVectors.title: Senegal-linked trade corridors
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia depends heavily on access through Senegal for trade, transport, and energy, giving Dakar substantial practical leverage over Banjul's economic choices.

frictionVectors.title: Tourism and external finance exposure
frictionVectors.details: Tourism, remittances, and donor-backed infrastructure provide essential foreign exchange but leave the country vulnerable to external demand, financing conditions, and investor priorities.

highlights: Gold remains the core sovereign-resource battleground

frictionVectors.title: Gold and illegal mining pressure
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale and informal mining generate foreign exchange but also environmental damage and smuggling risks, while foreign firms and trading networks retain significant influence over the value chain.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Prospective lithium development is attracting competing Western, Chinese, and regional interests as Accra attempts to secure local processing and avoid repeating a raw-export model.

highlights: Bauxite power is converting into infrastructure leverage

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite and Simandou concession politics
frictionVectors.details: The authorities are using major mining projects to demand roads, railways, ports, and larger state benefits, but dependence on foreign consortia leaves bargaining power uneven.

frictionVectors.title: China-Western strategic competition
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, and Western actors are competing for access to Guinea's minerals and logistics corridors, increasing external leverage while the junta restricts political accountability.

highlights: Cashew exports anchor a fragile economy

frictionVectors.title: Cashew-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign buyers and regional trading networks capture much of the value from raw cashews, while limited processing capacity keeps producers exposed to external price and demand shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Port and illicit-trafficking vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and contested political authority leave the port and maritime routes vulnerable to transnational trafficking networks and external security influence.

highlights: Ports and minerals remain strategic leverage

frictionVectors.title: External financing pressure
frictionVectors.details: Kenya remains reliant on multilateral lenders and foreign bond markets, limiting policy autonomy while fiscal reforms generate domestic backlash. Debt-service demands compete with development spending and sovereignty-sensitive infrastructure priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Mombasa and the Lamu corridor are contested through regional trade competition and foreign-backed infrastructure interests. Nairobi is balancing diversification of logistics partners against concerns over strategic dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Highlands water asymmetry
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water exports to South Africa provide essential revenue but bind the kingdom to South African infrastructure, pricing, and security interests. Delays and cost pressures in water-transfer projects expose the limits of Lesotho's bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector concentration
frictionVectors.details: Diamond operations generate foreign exchange but leave the state exposed to volatile global prices and foreign capital decisions. Local value addition and fiscal capture remain weaker than the country's resource potential.

highlights: Concessions drive growth, sovereignty concerns persist
Port and mineral corridors attract competition

frictionVectors.title: Resource concession imbalance
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, gold, forestry, and agricultural concessions remain central to Liberia's revenue model, but weak domestic processing reduces national capture of value. Contract transparency and community benefit-sharing continue to shape political risk.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign operators and investors remain important to port modernization and export corridors. This supports infrastructure delivery while limiting Monrovia's control over strategic logistics and associated revenue streams.

highlights: Oil wealth remains divided by rival authorities
Foreign security patrons shape energy access

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented oil governance
frictionVectors.details: Competing political and armed networks continue to contest control over the National Oil Corporation, terminals, and export routes. Production can be disrupted by local bargaining, making formal state sovereignty weaker than Libya's resource endowment suggests.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military and commercial influence
frictionVectors.details: External states support rival Libyan power centers and seek influence over energy, reconstruction, and security arrangements. This internationalizes domestic disputes and constrains unified control of strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Mining dependence and value leakage
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, gemstones, and other mineral projects are dominated by foreign capital and export-oriented supply chains. Madagascar is seeking greater fiscal and local-processing benefits while managing investor uncertainty and community opposition.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal extraction and forest pressure
frictionVectors.details: Illicit mining, precious-wood trafficking, and weak oversight undermine state control across remote areas. Enforcement gaps create openings for criminal networks and external buyers to capture value from strategic natural assets.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Malawi is courting investment in uranium, rare earths and other minerals, but limited fiscal capacity weakens its bargaining position with foreign developers and lenders.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Import Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Fuel shortages, foreign-exchange constraints and reliance on external budget support continue to limit sovereign control over transport, energy and agricultural supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Contract Confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The junta is pursuing greater state participation and revenue from gold, producing recurring disputes with international mining companies and increasing investment risk.

frictionVectors.title: Russian and AES Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Security cooperation with Russia and tighter alignment with Burkina Faso and Niger provide regime support but deepen exposure to external military, logistical and political influence.

frictionVectors.title: GTA Gas Project Exposure
frictionVectors.details: The offshore Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal offers major revenue potential, but its cross-border infrastructure and foreign operators constrain near-term national control.

frictionVectors.title: Iron and Green-Hydrogen Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mauritania is attracting Gulf, European and Chinese capital into mining and renewable infrastructure, creating opportunities while risking enclave development and uneven local benefits.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos Settlement Implementation
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius is advancing its sovereignty claim over the Chagos Archipelago, but the future of strategic facilities and the role of external powers remain sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Maritime Competition
frictionVectors.details: Indian Ocean port, surveillance and logistics initiatives bring investment and security benefits while increasing pressure to balance Indian, Western, Chinese and regional interests.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Legitimacy
frictionVectors.details: Morocco's control and development of Western Sahara underpin its Atlantic strategy but remain contested by Algeria and the Polisario Front, complicating external investment and trade.

frictionVectors.title: Water and Green-Hydrogen Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Large renewable and desalination projects can strengthen strategic autonomy, yet their dependence on foreign capital, technology and water-intensive industrial demand creates new vulnerabilities.

frictionVectors.title: CABO DELGADO LNG SECURITY
frictionVectors.details: Insurgency and reliance on foreign security support constrain Maputo's effective control over gas assets. International operators retain significant leverage over project timing and operating conditions.

frictionVectors.title: RESOURCE REVENUE AND DEBT PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Expectations for LNG revenues are colliding with fiscal stress and opaque contracting concerns. External lenders and investors continue to shape infrastructure and revenue priorities.

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE OIL OWNERSHIP
frictionVectors.details: Major offshore discoveries are drawing international oil companies into a sector where Namibia is still building regulatory and technical capacity. The government faces pressure to secure stronger local benefits without deterring investment.

frictionVectors.title: GREEN HYDROGEN INFRASTRUCTURE
frictionVectors.details: Large foreign-backed hydrogen projects depend on export corridors, concessional finance, and external technology. Delays or unfavorable offtake terms could limit domestic value capture.

highlights: Russian security ties replace Western partners

frictionVectors.title: URANIUM AND MINING RENEGOTIATION
frictionVectors.details: Niamey is seeking greater control and revenue from uranium and other minerals while relations with French-linked operators deteriorate. Weak administrative capacity and export dependence limit the gains from resource nationalism.

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Expanded reliance on Russian security personnel and equipment provides an alternative to Western partnerships but creates new political and operational dependencies. Insecurity continues to threaten mining corridors and energy infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: NIGER DELTA OIL THEFT
frictionVectors.details: Pipeline vandalism, illegal refining, and militant activity continue to reduce state capture of petroleum revenues. Foreign operators remain exposed while federal and local enforcement capacity is uneven.

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN CAPITAL AND GAS INFRASTRUCTURE
frictionVectors.details: Nigeria needs international finance and technical partnerships to expand gas processing, pipelines, and offshore production. Contract uncertainty and currency pressure weaken Abuja's bargaining position with investors.

frictionVectors.title: EASTERN DRC MINERAL SUPPLY CHAINS
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's alleged support for M23 has intensified scrutiny of cross-border mineral flows and raised the risk of sanctions or supply-chain restrictions. Kigali denies enabling illicit extraction and presents its posture as a security response.

frictionVectors.title: DONOR AND SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda retains strong domestic control but depends on external aid, peacekeeping revenue, and security partnerships. Western pressure over Congo policy could narrow its diplomatic and economic room for maneuver.

highlights: Small-state balancing in the Gulf of Guinea

frictionVectors.title: Unproven Offshore Hydrocarbons
frictionVectors.details: Exploration in the joint development zone with Nigeria has not yet delivered dependable commercial production. Expectations of future oil revenue continue to shape external partnerships and domestic fiscal planning.

frictionVectors.title: External Dependence on Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: São Tomé relies heavily on Portuguese, European, Chinese, and other external partners for transport, energy, and public finance. This expands development options but limits autonomous bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and Gas Contract Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: New offshore production offers Senegal greater fiscal leverage, but contract reviews and local-content demands risk friction with international operators and lenders. The central challenge is converting resource income into transparent, domestically controlled development.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Strategic Infrastructure Competition
frictionVectors.details: Dakar and emerging logistics corridors attract Gulf, European, Chinese, and Turkish capital. Dependence on external financing for ports, rail, and energy infrastructure creates long-term exposure to creditor and operator influence.

highlights: Blue economy remains the sovereignty anchor

frictionVectors.title: Maritime Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles depends on external naval, surveillance, and coast-guard support to protect its vast maritime zone from piracy, trafficking, and illegal fishing. Partnerships with India, Europe, and other actors strengthen capacity while complicating strategic neutrality.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Investment in Strategic Assets
frictionVectors.details: Tourism, fisheries, ports, and renewable-energy projects attract outside capital that is essential to the economy. The government must prevent investment concentration from eroding control over critical infrastructure or marine resources.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore and Mineral Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale mining remains central to exports and fiscal expectations, leaving the state vulnerable to commodity cycles and the negotiating power of foreign operators. Local processing, contract transparency, and environmental safeguards remain unresolved sovereignty issues.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Influence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed port, road, and energy projects are important for mining logistics and national connectivity. Their financing and operating terms can prioritize export corridors over broader domestic industrial development.

frictionVectors.title: Ports and Security Patronage
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, and other partners retain significant influence through military, port, training, and infrastructure arrangements. These relationships provide essential capacity but can compete with federal authority and produce rival external alignments.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Resource Governance
frictionVectors.details: Prospective oil and gas development is complicated by federal-state disputes, weak regulatory capacity, and insecurity. Without a credible revenue-sharing and licensing framework, future extraction could intensify political fragmentation rather than strengthen sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-policy uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is seeking greater domestic processing and value capture from platinum-group metals, manganese, and other strategic minerals, but regulatory uncertainty and infrastructure bottlenecks deter some investment.

frictionVectors.title: Electricity and logistics stress
frictionVectors.details: Grid instability and constraints at Transnet railways and ports reduce sovereign control over mineral export capacity and increase reliance on private and external capital.

highlights: Oil revenue remains the fiscal lifeline

frictionVectors.title: Oil-export vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan remains heavily dependent on oil transported through Sudan, leaving revenues exposed to pipeline disruption, Sudan's conflict, and negotiations over transit fees and security.

frictionVectors.title: Elite and external resource capture
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions, armed competition, and opaque contracting limit public control over oil and land resources while neighboring states and foreign firms retain significant leverage.

highlights: Red Sea access gains strategic value

frictionVectors.title: Competing control of gold
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling finance rival armed networks, while foreign-linked traders and regional intermediaries compete for access to Sudan's mineral revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Port and pipeline vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Conflict threatens Port Sudan, oil-export infrastructure, and supply corridors, increasing dependence on external security, logistics, and humanitarian actors.

frictionVectors.title: Investor leverage over critical minerals
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is tightening local-processing and beneficiation expectations for graphite, nickel, and other minerals, but project finance and technology remain dependent on foreign partners.

frictionVectors.title: Port-corridor sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Expansion of Dar es Salaam and proposed energy and transport corridors could strengthen regional influence, while concession terms and external financing remain politically sensitive.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional trade hub

frictionVectors.title: Port dependence and external finance
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's strategic role in Gulf of Guinea trade supports state revenue, but port expansion and logistics capacity rely heavily on foreign operators, lenders, and shipping networks.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate-sector governance
frictionVectors.details: Togo retains formal control over phosphate resources, yet limited downstream processing and opaque commercial arrangements constrain domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: EU migration and finance conditionality
frictionVectors.details: European funding and diplomatic engagement remain closely tied to migration control, giving Brussels significant leverage over Tunisian policy. Domestic concerns over sovereignty and treatment of migrants continue to sharpen tensions.

frictionVectors.title: Energy dependence and infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains dependent on imported energy and vulnerable to disruptions in gas and electricity connections with Algeria and Europe. Fiscal constraints limit its ability to rapidly expand sovereign energy capacity.

frictionVectors.title: East African Crude Oil Pipeline
frictionVectors.details: Uganda's oil export strategy depends on the Tanzania-linked pipeline, whose financing, environmental objections, and external political scrutiny have delayed development. The project could strengthen state revenues but also deepen reliance on foreign operators and lenders.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure and debt exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain important in transport and energy construction, while Uganda faces pressure to preserve fiscal space amid large infrastructure obligations. Kampala is balancing Chinese capital against Western and Gulf investment alternatives.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of copper value chains
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is seeking greater domestic processing, revenue capture, and transparency while relying on foreign capital to expand copper and cobalt production. Competition among Chinese, Gulf, European, and North American investors limits Lusaka's bargaining room.

frictionVectors.title: Debt restructuring constraints
frictionVectors.details: Debt treatment and creditor oversight continue to shape public investment and mining policy. Fiscal reform may improve long-term sovereignty but restricts near-term spending on power, rail, and local industrial capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Critical minerals and opaque external partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Lithium, platinum, gold, and other minerals attract Chinese, Emirati, and regional investors, but limited domestic processing leaves Zimbabwe exposed to external pricing and financing power. Regulatory uncertainty and opaque deals weaken the state's ability to secure durable local value.

frictionVectors.title: Currency and sanctions pressure
frictionVectors.details: Persistent currency instability and restricted access to international finance undermine planning for infrastructure and resource development. Harare's search for alternative financing partners increases dependence on politically aligned external actors.
